title: Lamentations
text:
Lamentations 1:1 Eikhah1[1] INTRODUCTIONEikhah — Lamentations — is a work that struggles with national theodicy. Five poems, each cast in unique literary form, present the destruction of Jerusalem as viewed through competing theological lenses. The work’s objective is not dissimilar to that of the Book of Job: where Job stages a contest between rival explanations of individual suffering, Eikhah stages the same contest at the national level. How could such catastrophe befall the Judean people if they are providentially shepherded by their God? Perhaps the strongest proof that the work of Eikhah articulates a question lies in its literary framing. The work begins with a question — “Eikhah” (איכה) — meaning “How is it conceivable?” or “How is it possible?” This same question, “Eikhah,” opens Chapters 2 and 4 as well, reinforcing the interrogative posture throughout. The work also ends with a question. After asserting the eternity of God’s existence and governance — “You, YHWH, are an eternal presence; Your throne endures from generation to generation” — the community voice their perplexion: “Why have You forgotten us for what seems like eternity? Why have You forsaken us for so many days?” This literary architecture frames the entire composition as an extended examination of divine providence and specifically national theodicy: If YHWH is the eternal shepherd of the Jewish people, why are His flocks continually devoured? DebtsThis work is both a development of and a divergence from Rabbi Joshua Berman’s scholarship on Eikhah. It agrees with three of his fundamental premises: that Eikhah, while composed of five different poems, is a single cohesive work; that within each poem a sophisticated dialogue unfolds, detectable through semantic and literary clues; and that Eikhah explores multiple angles of the cognitions and moods of the traumatised victims of the destruction of Jerusalem.It diverges from his theses that a gradual healing process unfolds as the work progresses, and that the primary transition is the community’s admission of guilt, facilitated by the narrator’s empathetic counselling. Instead, I postulate that the poems do not depict progress and healing. Rather, each poem presents a distinct configuration of the theological crisis, and the work as a whole deliberately resists resolution. Four Markers of Changing VoiceI believe that there are four key markers for distinguishing the theological voices at play:The differential use of the divine name. Throughout the poems the author dances between conceptions of YHWH and Adonai.The mode of address — to whom and about whom the voice speaks. Whether to the community, hostile neighbouring nations or God. If to God, whether the tone of the communication is supplicatory, accusatory, or intimate.The apportionment of responsibility for evil between man and God — whether suffering is conceived as divine punishment, divine withdrawal, or human consequence.The centrality of sin in a voice’s narrative — whether transgression is foregrounded, acknowledged in passing, or refused outright.A methodological note on voice identification. The primary markers are formal and linguistic (i.e., 1-2) rather than thematic content based (3-4). In other words, voice shifts are mostly identified through changes in grammatical person (third person to first, singular to plural), shifts in addressee (speaking to YHWH vs. speaking about YHWH; speaking to the nations vs. speaking to the community), and the divine name employed. Thus, the theological characterisation of each voice follows from, rather than drives, literary voice identifications. Thus, with but the odd outlier, this framework is not imposing theological categories onto the text and then finding voices to match them; but detecting voice shifts through linguistic markers and then characterising the theology each voice articulates.Two Fundamental OrientationsAcross Eikhah, I discern two fundamental theological orientations — the Adonaist and the Yahwist — key aspects of which persist to this day within various Orthodox Jewish theologies and communities.The Adonaist conceives of the relationship between God and Israel as essentially contractual: obedience is rewarded with blessing, disobedience with punishment. There is no pastoral dimension to this theology, no fatherly love, no covenantal intimacy. God is master, and man is subject. When catastrophe strikes, the Adonaist is shocked by its scale but not by its logic. Punishment is what God does when the terms of the contract are breached.The Yahwist, by contrast, conceives of God as a benevolent, pastoral father whose relationship with Israel is covenantal and intimate, infinitely transcending the bureaucracy of the formal religious contract. Within this broader Yahwist orientation, various distinct positions emerge as they wrestle with the theodicy problem:Agency and evil. Can the benevolent YHWH ever be the agent of evil, or must He maximally withdraw His protective providence, leaving the community exposed to the natural brutality of the geopolitical landscape? According to the second view, suffering is real but it is not God’s handiwork — it is the random consequence of divine absence. This position makes God less fearsome, but strips meaning from the specifics of suffering. In the poems, we find some Yahwists adopting the former position, and some the latter.Providence and the long view. Assuming that YHWH can be the agent of evil, does this necessarily undermine the conception of Him as benevolent and pastoral? If one adopts a long-term view, perhaps one will witness how YHWH ultimately ties everything back together — how suffering that was unbearable in the present was the necessary catalyst of future redemption. Thus, providence, however painful in the interim, may always benevolently steer history towards a good outcome.Epistemological humility. Can a shortsighted mortal expect to fathom the eternal divine script? Who is to say that what at first seemed the epitome of darkness was not in fact the harbinger of great light? Moreover, perhaps one can and should embrace paradoxical notions that transcend human intellect, and simultaneously entertain logical opposites. This is particularly relevant to the paradoxical view advanced at the end of Chapter 3 that is not dissimilar to the paradoxical philosophy of Ramchal (Rabbi Moshe Chaim Luzzato) in Da’at Tevunot #54 through #56.The limits of the covenant. Behind the scenes lurk a further pair of more subtle and terrifying questions. First: Are there limits to YHWH’s covenantal pastoral care, or can one overstep the red lines and provoke YHWH into reneging on His contract — or worse still, lashing out at His disloyal former partner? Second: Are there limits to how far YHWH will go? When meting out providential punishment, will YHWH architect sadism and barbarity? Will YHWH act in a self-defeating way and allow His own institutions to be profaned? Likewise, even if one entertains that YHWH merely withdraws His providence, are there limits to the atrocities in the face of which He is willing to remain silent?DisclaimersI acknowledge the risk of anachronism when projecting God-concepts distilled over the millennia onto Judeans who lived two and a half millennia ago, though I am unsure whether advancing a theological framework exacerbates this risk over and above any other theoretical framework.Limitations of the Adonaist/Yahwist model: The divine-name criterion holds consistently across all five poems with only three exceptions, all of which are flagged in the footnotes. In Poem II, there are two instances of an Adonaist invoking YHWH surrounding the festival at the Temple of Zion. In Poem III, the Yahwist gever invokes Adonai, although there he appears as a metaphor for his guardian defender. I contend that three flagged exceptions across five poems do not undermine a rule; they confirm its general applicability and challenge the reader to choose between considering context-specific nuance (as I have done) or providing an interpretation for deliberate messiness in the specific context. These options are discussed more extensively in the relevant places.The Arc of the WorkThese two theological orientations — and the sub-positions within them — do not simply appear once and fall silent. They recur, recombine, and recollide across all five poems, producing a shifting kaleidoscope of theological crisis. It is worth sketching the arc of the entire work before entering the poems themselves, so that the reader can perceive both the distinctiveness of each poem and the threads that bind them.The first poem functions as an overture. The narrator surveys the devastation of the community’s three personified dimensions — Jerusalem (its political statehood), Judea (its populace and culture), and Zion (its Temple and religious life) — and then yields the floor to each in turn. Jerusalem cries out to YHWH who disappeared with calamitous consequence; Zion speaks about YHWH with accusatory distance; and Judea takes refuge in the punitive theology of Adonai. The poem closes with tentative, fragile steps towards reconciliation: each persona, cornered by the narrator’s critiques, edges towards a holistic view that vindicates YHWH and acknowledges sin.The second poem escalates the crisis by staging four initially disparate theological voices. An Adonaist catalogues God’s devastation institution by institution, naming Adonai as the agent of every act of destruction. A Yahwist responds by detailing the same collapse from his own vantage point — focusing on the systematic dismantling of providential protections rather than the perpetration of atrocities. A humanist voice then breaks through with raw, theology-rejecting grief over the suffering of mothers and infants. Finally, a second Yahwist insists that YHWH was actively executing a prophetically foretold punishment. Where the first poem allowed each voice its discrete monologue, the second forces them into proximity — and ultimately into convergence. The poem’s climactic achievement is a choral synthesis in which all four voices, unable to sustain their individual frameworks in the face of such suffering, unite in a single anguished address that interweaves elements of every position. The poem’s final identification of God as “the Enemy” marks the nadir of Eikhah’s theological despair.The third poem responds to this nadir by introducing the gever — who I believe to be the gever of Psalm 94 — whose forward-facing Yahwist theology offers balm precisely where the backward-looking theology of sin-and-punishment had failed. The gever does not deny the severity of suffering, for he has endured it viscerally. Yet he reframes it as the necessary harbinger of future redemption, insisting that YHWH’s kindness never ceases and His mercies are never exhausted — even when YHWH Himself appears to be the agent of affliction. This is the poem’s most revolutionary claim: that YHWH’s benevolence is unfailing and all-pervasive, and that what appears as cruelty in the present is the necessary catalyst of salvation, though how this is so will only become apparent in the unforetold future. Alongside this Yahwist hope, an Adonaist voice provides a complementary comfort: Adonai’s punishments, however harsh, are fundamentally just and educational rather than vindictive. However, as the poem advances and the traumatised community attempts to assimilate these teachings, their effort rapidly disintegrates into theological confusion along with accusation and bitterness — a failed integration that testifies to the depth of their trauma. They are emotionally incapable of portraying their horrific encounters as educational and constructive, let alone benevolent. The poem thus concludes with a gever-like speaker who offers an alternative theology, in which he synthesises YHWH’s passive disengagement and active providence into a paradoxical but sustaining framework, whose vengeful fury is directed not at God but at the human agents of persecution.The fourth poem marks a dramatic shift in register. Here there is no theological debate, no cognitive wrestling with God-concepts. The speakers — a narrator-observer and the community — are frozen in the psychosomatic dimension of trauma: they recount scenes of starvation, degradation, and cannibalism with the numb intensity of witnesses who have not yet begun to process what they have seen. Ironically, it is precisely this cognitive paralysis that protects their theology from the dissonance of earlier poems. The poem’s most theologically significant contribution is its unfiltered exposure of Judea’s own moral corruption — the false prophets, the persecuted righteous, the zealously wicked — material that the more cognitively defended speakers of earlier poems could not articulate. A brief, cold, and prophetic third voice closes the poem with laconic assurance: Zion’s punishment is spent; Edom’s is coming — the cognitive clarity of prophetic promises barely register emotionally when faced with devastation and traumatic dissociation.The fifth and final poem is more prayer than poem. A Yahwist community describes its degradation to YHWH in graphic detail, pleading for the restoration of a providential relationship. Finally, the community overtly states the theological question that has underpinned the entire text: We assert the eternity of YHWH’s existence and governance! If so, how could YHWH have forsaken us for what seems like eternity? The community then float a second terrifying hypothesis as an afterthought, almost as a postscript, in the very last sentence of the work. Perhaps YHWH came to despise His people; perhaps YHWH has eternally abandoned them! Although they argue to reject this hypothesis, the author seems to have deliberately thrown this disturbing and likely hitherto suppressed thought into the mix at the very end to destabilize and undermine closure. Thereby, the author emphatically communicates that theodicy and its various implications can never be settled beyond a trace of doubt, and that those doubts can be deeply disturbing, gnawing at the heart and mind of the believer.Understood in this light, the synagogue custom of repeating the penultimate verse after the final one may represent the Jewish religionist’s resistance to entertaining the possibility of YHWH’s rejection; a desperate move to remain hopeful and forward-facing despite the doubts. In other words, the custom enacts in ritual practice a dialectic; resistance to closure on the one hand, with commitment to belief on the other. Taken together, the five poems do not narrate a journey from grief to healing, nor from denial to acceptance. Rather, they constitute five distinct explorations of national theodicy, each testing a different configuration of the relationship between divine character, human sin, and communal suffering. The work’s unity lies not in narrative progression but in its relentless return to the same unanswerable question: how could a providential God allow — or, worse, orchestrate — the annihilation of His own people? That the question remains unanswered at the close is not a failure of the work but its deepest theological statement: the struggle with theodicy is the permanent condition of the earthling subject.
Poem 12[2] The first poem functions as an overture to the entire work, establishing its Judean backdrop and context and much of its theological lexicon. It is the only poem that introduces and names each of the community’s three personified dimensions — Jerusalem, Judea, and Zion — and grants each a discrete monologue in which to articulate its distinctive theological stance.The Narrator’s Survey (vv. 1–6) The poem opens with a collected, rational narrator who surveys the devastation with something approaching clinical composure. He addresses each persona in sequence — Jerusalem the widowed political entity, Judea the exiled populace, and Zion the desolate religious centre — cataloguing the radical reversal of fortune that each has undergone. Crucially, this narrator is himself a Yahwist. He interprets the catastrophe through the lens of divine withdrawal: YHWH’s protective providence was suspended on account of excessive communal transgression, and the ensuing suffering was the natural consequence of geopolitical torrents taking their course, not the direct infliction of a punishing deity. Sin is central to his narrative, but punishment — in the strict sense of God actively striking — is not.Three Monologues (vv. 9c–16) The narrator then yields the floor to each persona in turn, who, in espousing their unique theological traumas, lay out their conception of the divine and retribution.Jerusalem (vv. 9c–11c) speaks directly to YHWH, employing His covenantal name in the vocative. She too is a Yahwist: she shares the narrator’s conviction that YHWH is fundamentally benevolent. Yet she grapples with the limits of the withdrawal model. How can YHWH sit idly by while the enemy desecrates His own Temple? Her mode of address is supplicatory, not accusatory — “Look, O YHWH” — but the urgency of her plea betrays a theological anxiety: if YHWH’s own sanctuary is not immune, what covenant remains?Zion (vv. 12–15) represents the most theologically traumatised voice in this poem. Significantly, she speaks about YHWH rather than to Him — addressing the surrounding nations instead, a marker of theological distance. Though she retains the covenantal name, her Yahwism has shifted: she posits YHWH as the active architect of suffering, the one who designed and implemented her affliction. Her tone is accusatory and anguished.Judea (vv. 13c–16) abandons the covenantal name altogether. She switches to Adonai — “My master” — conceiving of God not as a loving father but as a stern overlord. There is no pastoral warmth in her theology, no intimacy, no covenant to invoke. Like Zion, she speaks about God rather than to Him. Convinced that God is unwilling to comfort her, she sees punishment as simply what masters do when contracts are breached. Critique and Tentative Reconciliation (vv. 17–22) At this juncture, the narrator re-enters with a succinct, pointed critique of each persona’s coping strategy. Zion addressed the nations — but did they help? Judea rejected YHWH, failing to discern the fingerprints of long-term providence. Jerusalem was shocked by YHWH’s inaction, but she had not acknowledged, let alone repented for, her sinfulness.Cornered by these critiques, the three personas take tentative, fragile steps towards reconciliation. Zion, still unable to address YHWH directly, at least recognises her rebelliousness and concedes that YHWH acted fairly — while hoping that the same providence will hold her oppressors accountable. Jerusalem beseeches YHWH once more but this time openly confesses guilt. Finally, Judea ventures the most significant development: she finds the courage to address God directly, requesting that the same providential punishment she endured be visited upon her persecutors.These reconciliatory gestures are real but limited. They are intellectual concessions wrung from each persona under the pressure of the narrator’s logic, not settled convictions born of emotional resolution.
The narrator shares his observations,3[3] The narrator's voice is identified by third-person description of all three personas, speaking about all of them but to none of them. The divine name YHWH appears in the theological explanation (v. 5), consistent with a Yahwist orientation. beginning with Jerusalem: 4[4] In these first two verses he personifies a city, that intuitively maps onto the third persona identified as Jerusalem as the chapter unfolds.
How is it conceivable
That the city once teeming with people
Now sits isolated
Having become like a widow.
That she who was once the great one among the nations,
The noble among the provinces,
Has become a vassal laborer.

Lamentations 1:2 She weeps bitterly in the night —
Her tears lie undried on her cheeks,
For there are none to console her
Among all her lovers.
On the contrary:
All her friends have betrayed her;
They have become her enemies.

Lamentations 1:3 The narrator considers the reversal of fortune of Judea — the once free and innovative Judean people:
Judea has been exiled
For she was unable to bear the poverty and excessive labour
Wrought by her vassal status.
But when she attempted to settle among the nations,
She found no rest.
All who once trailed her
Have now overtaken her
As she navigates between the constraints imposed on her.

Lamentations 1:4 The narrator turns to Zion — the Temple and religious life of Mount Zion — once a vibrant spiritual centre:
The roads of Zion are mournful,
For they are now bereft of festival pilgrims.
All her gates are desolate,
For her elders and scholars are no longer.
Her priests groan rather than chant the service;
Her young women grieve rather than rejoice;
Her lot is bitter rather than sweet.

Lamentations 1:5 Her oppressors have taken the lead;
Her enemies have enjoyed serenity;
For YHWH had her grieve5[5] Perhaps these three clauses can be associated with the three personas, but additional textual evidence is required.
For her excessive transgressions.
With YHWH’s departure — the community’s inner spirit — its external beauty and dignity likewise drained from each persona.
Her (Judea’s) beautiful infants were marched into captivity,
Before the oppressor
To be exploited and to advance his interests.

Lamentations 1:6 Likewise,
All dignity departed the community of Zion.
Her talented officials have become redundant —
Like harts that find no pasture;
They too now march
Depleted of strength
Before those who once trailed her.

Lamentations 1:7 Jerusalem now remembers —
In her days of poverty and downtroddenness —
All that she treasured in bygone times.
How when her people fell into the hand of the oppressor
No one came to her assistance;
How her oppressors had looked on
And mocked the suspension of her grandeur.

Lamentations 1:8 The Yahwist narrator once more points to sin as the cause, explaining the community’s degradation as a natural process:
Jerusalem sinned grievously,
She therefore became contemptible;
All who once honoured her now belittle her,
For she has been laid bare;
She too groaned
As she came undone.

Lamentations 1:9 Her filth was paraded on her skirt hems;
For she gave no thought to her future.
Is it thus surprising
That she has sunk to such depths
With none to comfort her!?
Jerusalem now addresses YHWH directly — a Yahwist who shares the narrator’s conviction that YHWH is benevolent. Yet she grapples with the limits of the withdrawal model: how can YHWH sit idly by while the enemy desecrates His own Temple?
Look, O YHWH at my affliction,6[6] Markers of voice shift: the grammatical person switches abruptly from the narrator’s third person to direct second-person address of YHWH in the vocative (“Look, O YHWH”). The divine name is YHWH, not Adonai. The addressee is God Himself, not the nations or the community. This combination — direct address, covenantal name, supplicatory tone — identifies the speaker as a Yahwist who expects YHWH’s benevolent intervention. The voice is identified as Jerusalem since the narrator was interrupted mid-verse while describing Jerusalem.
Do You not see
That the enemy has become great!

Lamentations 1:10 Look how the oppressor has stretched his hand
Over all Zion’s7[7] The identification of Zion is evident from its association with the sanctuary and its laws forbidding alien access. That Zion is the temple complex was evident earlier in verse 4. treasures;
She has even witnessed nations
Invade her sanctuary,
Those whom You forbade
To enter Your congregation.

Lamentations 1:11 Look how all Judea’s8[8] This identification is intuitive, but not necessary. It follows the assumption that the populace are associated exclusively with Judea rather than Zion. people groan
As they search for bread;
How they must trade their treasures for food
To revive their lives.
Look, O YHWH, and consider
How belittled I have become.

Lamentations 1:12 Zion — theologically traumatised — now speaks. Unlike Jerusalem, she speaks about YHWH rather than to Him, a mark of her theological distance. Her Yahwism posits YHWH as the active architect of her suffering: 9[9] Markers of voice shift: the addressee changes from YHWH to the passersby (“you all passersby”), with the speaker speaking about YHWH in the third person (“YHWH had me suffer”) rather than to Him. The divine name remains YHWH, indicating she is still a Yahwist, but the shift from second-person address to third-person reference signals theological distancing. This is consistent with the content of her address that shifts in tone from supplicatory to accusatory. The identification of the speaker as Zion can be deduced in a two-step process; first elimination, then deliberation. Elimination: the chapter employs three personas and a narrator. The narrator is ruled out due to the first-person usage, and Jerusalem is ruled out since it offered the previous speech. Deliberation: Of the remaining two speakers, one is clearly Adonaist and the other clearly Yahwist. The human-focused content of the Adonaist speech along with the narrator’s critiques in verse 19 suggest that Zion maps better onto the Yahwist voice.
May no such fate befall you all passersby.
Consider and look:
Is there any agony as intense as my agony —
That was deliberately delivered to me!?
Like the grief YHWH had me suffer
On the day His wrath flared!?

Lamentations 1:13 For, from on high
He sent fire into my bones
And hammered them.
He spread a net for my feet to ensnare me;
He made me come undone.
He made me devastated;
Sickened all day long.

Lamentations 1:14 Judea, brutalised and humiliated, adopts the Adonaist view. She switches from YHWH to Adonai — “My master” — conceiving of God as a stern overlord, not a loving father. There is no pastoral warmth, no covenant to invoke. Like Zion, she speaks about God rather than to Him. 10[10] Markers of voice shift: the divine name switches from YHWH to Adonai (“My master”). The theological content also shifts to address sinfulness. The rationale for the voice’s identification as Judea appears in the previous footnote.
The yoke of my transgressions
Lay exposed in His hand
There, they grew, entangled,
Gradually climbing over my neck,
And sapping my strength.
Adonai — my master — has delivered me into hands
From which I cannot possibly rise again.

Lamentations 1:15 Adonai trampled all my strongmen
In my midst.
He proclaimed a festival
For shattering my young men.
Adonai has trodden as in a winepress
The Judean community’s young women.

Lamentations 1:16 For these things I weep;
Tears relentlessly tumble from my eyes;
For a comforter who might revive my spirit
Has distanced themself from me.
My children have become desolate,
For the enemy has overpowered us.

Lamentations 1:17 The narrator now critiques each persona’s coping strategy. Zion addressed the nations — but did they help? Judea rejected YHWH, failing to discern long-term providence. Jerusalem was shocked by YHWH’s inaction, yet had not acknowledged her sinfulness.11[11] Markers of voice shift: the grammatical person reverts to third person who speaks about the three personas, signaling the narrator’s return. As expected, the divine name reverts to YHWH. The addressee is once again the audience, not God, the personas or the nations.
Zion stretches her hands to her contemporaries,
But none provide her with comfort.
YHWH had providentially commanded from time immemorial that Jacob — the Judeans
Be surrounded by his oppressors.
Jerusalem has become contemptible among them.

Lamentations 1:18 Cornered by the narrator’s critiques, each of the three personas take tentative steps toward reconciliation — acknowledging sin and attempting to justify YHWH’s behaviour within their former frameworks.
Zion, still unable to address YHWH, concedes her rebelliousness and that YHWH acted fairly — her tone now hurt rather than angry. She hopes the same tough providence will hold her oppressors accountable for their misdeeds. She again addresses the nations: 12[12] Markers of voice shift: this speaker employs the first person, and once more the address is to the nations. The style of address – about YHWH but to the nations is consistent with Zion’s voice in her previous speech. However, her tone has shifted from accusatory anger to conceding YHWH’s justice.
YHWH is in the right,
For I have rebelled against His word.
Listen here — take heed — all you peoples:
Look at my agony —
At my young women and young men
Who have gone into captivity.

Lamentations 1:19 At how I called to my lovers,
Yet they deceived me;
At how my priests and scholarly elders perished in the city
While searching for food to revive their lives.
Is this not unprecedented and providential?
Beware! That same providence shall come back to bite you!

Lamentations 1:20 Jerusalem again beseeches YHWH, but this time openly confesses guilt: 13[13] Markers of voice shift: the return to direct second-person address of YHWH (“Look, O YHWH”) identifies Jerusalem, resuming her characteristic mode from v. 9. Both the covenantal name used in the vocative and the request that YHWH “look” are consistent with her former style. The new element is the confession (“I have been very rebellious”) — consistent with the critique the narrator specifically levelled at Jerusalem.
Look, O YHWH,
For I am distressed;
My gut is wrenched.
I have experienced a change of heart,
For I accept that I have been very rebellious.
Look! Outdoors, the sword brings bereavement,
Indoors, it is like death.

Lamentations 1:21 Look at how they heard that I was groaning,
Yet no one comforted me.
On the contrary —
All my enemies heard of my trouble and delighted
Because, to their minds, You had done it.
Please, restore Your providence:
Bring on the day You announced,
When they will be as I am now.

Lamentations 1:22 Judea now finds the courage to address God directly, requesting that equally harsh punishment be visited upon her persecutors: 14[14] Markers of voice shift: This speaker shift has been imposed top-down on the text, since it could read as the continuation of Jerusalem’s plea. If so, one would entertain that Judea rebuffed the narrator’s critique and stormed away from the discussion – thus leaving the third persona’s account without closure. This is plausible. However, I opted for a less dramatic finale, in which the third of the three personas – which, by process of elimination, is Judea, makes her final speech.
Let all their evil doings come before You,
And deliberately deliver punishment to them
Like You deliberately delivered punishment to me
For of all my transgressions.
For they have made me suffer bitterly:
My groans are many and my heart is faint.

Lamentations 2:1 POEM II: The Convergence15[15] Where the first poem granted each theological voice its own discrete monologue, the second brings four initially disparate voices into proximity and, ultimately, into convergence. An Adonaist, a Yahwist who maintains the withdrawal model, a humanist who ignores theological frameworks altogether, and an accusatory Yahwist who posits active divine punishment, each speak in turn — the emotional weight of their presentations growing increasingly intense as the poem progresses. The poem concludes with a deliberately unsettled choral synthesis in which all four voices unite to process their trauma together.The Adonaist’s Opening (vv. 1–5) The poem opens with an Adonaist speaker cataloguing destruction, institution by institution. His use of Adonai is relentless and deliberate: Adonai is the named subject of every verb of devastation. Adonai shrouded Zion in storm clouds; Adonai devoured Jacob’s abodes without mercy; Adonai demolished the Judean strongholds. The Adonaist does not flinch from attributing aggression to God — indeed, it is the logic of his theology. The poem’s most striking early phrase has the Adonaist declare that Adonai “became like an enemy,” a formulation that will develop into openly naming Adonai “My Enemy” at its end.The Yahwist’s Response (vv. 6–10) The Yahwist responds by detailing the same destruction from his own theological vantage. He too catalogues the collapse of institutions — the Torah and its scholars, prophecy and its prophets, Jerusalem and her jubilant young women. Yet his framing is critically different. He focuses on the systematic dismantling of protections: the metaphorical walls, ramparts, gates, and locks that YHWH had once providentially erected around Judea. The dire consequences that followed were not the hand of YHWH but nature taking its course once Judea was rendered vulnerable. Between the lines, the Yahwist appears particularly perturbed by the methodical nature of the destruction — the image of YHWH stretching a plumb line before demolishing the walls suggests premeditated architectural precision — but he stops short of accusing YHWH of planning or perpetrating the resulting atrocities.The Humanist Interruption (vv. 11–13) At this juncture, a more personal, emotional voice breaks into the excessively rational dialogue. Rather than addressing the sterile “institutions” of Judea, this speaker brings into focus the acute fates of innocent individuals — the suffering of frail mothers and their dying children. He makes no mention of God at all. His voice is humanist in orientation, implicitly arguing for the impossibility of any satisfactory theological account of such darkness.The Punishing Yahwist (vv. 14–17) The humanist speaker is replaced by a critical, accusatory voice. This speaker is also a Yahwist, but one who believes YHWH was providentially active in punishment — executing a foretold scheme rather than merely withdrawing protection. He attacks the community for the false prophets who failed to expose their iniquity. In his view, the catastrophe was predicted in God’s earlier warnings in Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28, and YHWH has now carried out His threat.The Choral Synthesis (vv. 18–22) The poem’s final section is its most remarkable literary achievement. I think it is unfeasible — and indeed incorrect — to unravel these closing verses into individual speeches with unique theologies. Rather, close literary analysis reveals how this section was deliberately crafted to harmonise the divergent voices. When performed, it would have been recited in unison by all the speakers. Adonaist and Yahwist, theist and humanist, set aside their theological differences and listen together to the pained cries of Judea’s innocents. Their combined speech then succinctly intertwines elements of all their former viewpoints: they briefly invoke the human experience, attempt to tame the harshness of Adonai, seek to reengage with a withdrawn YHWH, and express vexation at the providential aggression of YHWH. What results is a theologically incoherent, though literarily lucid, jumble of verses. The synthesis is powerful and seems to communicate healing through solidarity in the absence of theological correction. Notably, the final verse, in which the singular “enemy” replaces the plural “enemies”, thus identifying God Himself as “the Enemy”, marks the nadir of the work’s theological despair.
The Adonaist begins:16[16] Markers of voice: the divine name is explicitly Adonai (used relentlessly in vv. 1–5). The subject-verb pattern depicts blazing anger and ruthless aggression. This speaker is thus overtly Adonaistic.
How is it conceivable
That Adonai in His anger
Shrouded the community of Zion in storm clouds!?
He threw down from heaven to earth
The glory of Israel;
He did not remember His footstool — the epicentre of His worldly manifestation
On the day of His anger.

Lamentations 2:2 Adonai devoured without mercy
All the fine abodes of Jacob;
In His wrath he demolished
The strongholds of the Judean community —
Toppling them to the ground.
He desecrated a kingdom and its officials.

Lamentations 2:3 He cut down in raging anger
The entire headship of Israel;
He withdrew His protective right hand
In the face of the enemy;
His rage blazed in Jacob like a flaming fire,
Consuming all around.

Lamentations 2:4 His protective right hand was not merely paralyzed — it persecuted:
He bent His bow like an enemy,
His right hand set about it like a foe.
He killed all those desirable to behold.
In the tent of the community of Zion
His fury was vented like fire.

Lamentations 2:5 Adonai became like an enemy:
He devoured Israel,
He devoured all its palaces,
And destroyed all its strongholds.
He advanced grief and mourning
Within the Judean community.

Lamentations 2:6 He laid bare His abode as though it were a garden;
He destroyed His place of commune.
He banished YHWH from Zion’s memory17[17] This speech contains two of three outliers that challenge the clean Adonaistic-Yahwistic framework, for twice the ostensible Adonaist invokes YHWH. When weighed against the overwhelming evidence in favor of this framework, I conclude that these instances do not undermine the framework but that each instance requires special treatment. One hypothesis – and the one I favor - is that even the Adonaist associates YHWH with the temple cult, and more specifically, with the festivals at the temple. Both of these YHWH references feature alongside temple festivities. Alternative hypotheses may explore themes of irony and sarcasm as conveyed by the deliberate use of the other’s deity concept. I note that my former hypothesis is only possible given the poet’s use of the causative form “shikakh” — “to cause to be forgotten.” The verse is thus open to interpretation, as to whether YHWH is the subject (“the causer”) or the object (“the caused”). Due to the context — that is, Adonai appearing as the subject in the following verse — I have opted to keep Adonai as the subject in this verse, interpreting YHWH as the object. Should one strongly object to this reading, the second hypothesis should be explored instead.;
He abolished its Shabbat and festival services.
In his ferocious anger
He spurned king and priest.

Lamentations 2:7 Adonai distanced Himself from His altar,
He Rejected His sanctuary.
He delivered the walls of Zion’s palaces
Into the hand of the enemy.
They raised a clamour in the house of YHWH18[18] See previous footnote. This is the second of three outliers.
As though it was a festival day.

Lamentations 2:8 The Yahwist responds. He too catalogues the destruction, but his framing differs: YHWH systematically dismantled the community’s providential protections — walls, ramparts, gates, leadership — but the resulting atrocities were nature taking its course once Judea was left vulnerable: 19[19] Markers of voice shift: the divine name switches from Adonai to YHWH. The subject-verb pattern shifts subtly (though If this were the only marker, it would be insufficient evidence for a change of speaker): where the Adonaist used active verbs of destruction with God as agent, the Yahwist focuses exclusively on the collapse of protections and the resulting mourning.
YHWH schemed to destroy
The protective wall of the community of Zion;
He planned meticulously
As though stretching a plumb line;
Then, He did not withhold His hand from devouring them.
He cast her protective walls and ramparts into mourning,
As they were made barren together.

Lamentations 2:9 Her gates sunk into the ground,
He decommissioned and broke her locks.
He let her leadership collapse:
Now her king and prince are exiled among the nations;
She has no religious counsel;
Even Her prophets cannot encounter a vision from YHWH.

Lamentations 2:10 Now the scholarly elders of the community of Zion
Sit on the ground;
They are silent.
They have heaved dirt onto their heads,
They have girded themselves with sackcloth.
Now the once proud young women of Jerusalem
Bow their heads to the ground in shame.

Lamentations 2:11 A personal, emotional voice breaks through. This speaker makes no mention of God. He focuses not on institutions but on innocent individuals — frail mothers and dying children. His voice is humanist, implicitly rejecting all theological frameworks. He addresses the Judeans directly, with empathy rather than analysis: 20[20] Markers of voice shift: The primary marker is the grammatical person switches abruptly to the first-person singular (“My eyes,” “My gut,” “My liver”). A secondary marker is the absence of divine names anywhere in these verses. Although verse 13 switches to the second person, I have opted not to invoke a fifth speaker to deliver it, since a single humanist tone shines through both verses 12 and 13, suggesting that the same speaker first speaks about himself before turning to address the Judeans.
My eyes are spent with weeping,
My gut is wrenched,
My liver is spilled on the ground,
Because of the destruction of my community;
At the writhing of its infants and suckling babes
In the main roads of the city.

Lamentations 2:12 They cry out to their mothers:
"Where is bread and wine?"
As they writhe like the dismembered
In the main roads of the city;
As their souls ebb away
In their mothers’ embrace.

What could be likened to your lot,
O community of Jerusalem?
To what can I compare your calamity,
That I may comfort you — O youthful community of Zion?
For your rupture is as vast as the sea!
Who can possibly heal you?

Lamentations 2:14 An accusatory Yahwist voice replaces the humanist. Unlike the earlier Yahwist, this speaker believes YHWH was providentially active in punishment — executing a scheme foretold in Leviticus and Deuteronomy: 21[21] Markers of voice shift: the empathetic tone shifts radically to an accusatory tone, though it is debatable whether this only occurs in verse 17 (Rabbi Berman suggests that verses 14-16 can be read sympathetically; I argue this is forced) or immediately in verse 14. Likewise, the divine name YHWH returns in verse 17 along with a providential theology, indicating the appearance of a Yahwist speaker. That this is not the reappearance of the earlier Yahwist is evident in the active aggression ascribed to YHWH, which was deliberately absent in the former Yahwist’s speech.
Forget not how your prophets depicted visions for you
That were false and unsubstantiated.
They did not expose your iniquity
So you could repent for your waywardness.
Instead they depicted false prophecies for you,
And manipulated their messages to cast you off.

Lamentations 2:15 It is thus only natural that at first:
All passersby clapped their hands at you;
They whistled and wagged their heads

Is this the city that they — our ancestors — would label:
The totality of beauty,
The joy of all the earth?

They declared: We have devoured her!
Is this not the day we longed for!?
At last, we have encountered and seen it!"

Lamentations 2:17 YHWH has perpetrated what He purposed.
He has carried out His threat

He exalted the antlers of your foes.

Lamentations 2:18 What follows is the poem’s most remarkable achievement: a choral synthesis in which all four voices, unable to sustain their individual frameworks, unite in a single anguished address. Adonaist and Yahwist, humanist and theist alike set aside their theses and listen to the cries of Judea’s innocents. Their combined speech intertwines elements of every position: human suffering, the harshness of Adonai, the withdrawal of YHWH, and the vexation of providential aggression. This communicates both ideological chaos and unity in suffering: 22[22] Markers of voice shift: A return to third-person description, along with all the evidence for deliberate synthesis and convergence of the four earlier speeches, as presented in the next footnote.,23[23] Verses 18 and 19 ring primarily humanist and Adonaist — indicated by the invocation of Adonai and thematic echoes of the humanist’s starvation-themed verses 11–12 — yet the wall metaphor hearkens back to the Yahwist in verse 8, and the imagery of rising upwards continues the Yahwist motif of the Judeans sunken to the ground in verses 9–10. Verse 20 unites all four positions. “Look and behold” had been the phrase of the withdrawal-Yahwist in Poem 1; “to whom You deliberately delivered this” voices active-providential Yahwism; the invocation of starving mothers hearkens back to the humanist; and “the sanctuary of Adonai” is openly Adonaist. Verses 21-22 also interweave divergent positions. Verse 21 and the first stanza of the 22 express vexation at YHWH as active aggressor – providential Yahwism, while invoking the first-person tone of the humanist (“my”). The final stanza speaks about YHWH — “on the day of YHWH’s anger” — rather than to him, perhaps a throwback to the third-person voice of the passive-withdrawal Yahwist earlier in this poem. The singular “enemy” rather than the plural “enemies” employed elsewhere in the work signals that God is here labelled “the Enemy,” hearkening back to the Adonaist portrayal “like an enemy” at the poem’s opening.
The starving infants cried out their hearts to Adonai!
O parents — wall of the Zion community!
Let your tears stream down like a creek
By day and by night!
Allow yourself no respite,
Your eyes no tranquility!

Lamentations 2:19 Arise and cry out in the night,
As the watchmen’s shifts begin!
Pour out your heart like water
Before the presence of Adonai!
Lift your hands to Him;
Implore Him for the lives of your children,
Who writhe with hunger
At the head of every street.

Lamentations 2:20 Look, O YHWH, and behold
To whom you deliberately delivered this!
Should women eat their offspring,
Those who they delivered and nurture!?
Should priest and prophet be killed
In the "sanctuary of Adonai"?

Lamentations 2:21 The young and old are laid on the dirt of the streets;
My young women and my young men were felled by the sword.
You massacred on the day of your anger;
You butchered and showed no pity.

Lamentations 2:22 You summoned my enemies from all around
As though for a day of festival!
On the day of YHWH’s anger,
There was neither refugee nor remnant.
Those whom I nurtured and reared,
My enemy consumed.

Lamentations 3:1 POEM III: The Gever’s Balm24[24] The third poem is the longest and most theologically ambitious of the five. It is the structural and theological centrepiece of Eikhah, and its triple acrostic form (three verses per Hebrew letter) perhaps indicates that the poet recognises it to be the work’s backbone. Perhaps the poem responds directly to the catastrophic and chaotic conclusion of the second poem that culminated in the labelling of God as “My Enemy” by introducing a new voice, the gever, whose forward-facing Yahwist theology offers healing where the backward-looking theology of sin-and-punishment had failed. The gever’s central teaching is that YHWH’s kindness never ceases and His mercies are never exhausted — even when suffering is most acute, even when YHWH Himself appears to be its author, even when YHWH expresses what is ostensibly the very opposite of benevolence. This insistence on unfailing divine benevolence, maintained alongside the attribution of all suffering to YHWH, is the poem’s most distinctive and ambitious theological claim, albeit one that has echoes elsewhere in Scripture.The Gever’s Testimony (vv. 1–30) The poem opens with a speaker who identifies himself as “the gever” — that I take to mean the gever we have already encountered elsewhere in scripture — in Psalm 94: “Fortunate is the gever who is chastised by YH that He may teach him from His Torah. To offer him quiet from the nasty waters, while He excavates the abyss for the wicked. For YHWH will not cast-off His people nor reject His inheritance… Were not YHWH my help, I would in an instant dwell in silence. If I think my foot has given way, Your kindness, O YHWH, supports me. When I am filled with inner turmoil, Your assurance soothes my soul. Shall the seat of injustice be Your partner…? They band together to do away with the righteous; they condemn the innocent to death. But YHWH is my fortress; my God is my sheltering rock. Their evil will be made to recoil upon them, through their own wickedness they will be annihilated; YHWH our God will annihilate them.” There too, the Psalmist extrapolates from the individual suffering to national suffering, and there too, theodicy is viewed through a forward-facing lens.(The identification of this figure with the gever of Psalm 94 warrants elaboration. I suggest it because the parallels are dense and specific. Firstly, the identifier: the Psalmist chooses gever — not ish, not adam — to name the sufferer, exactly as our poet does. Secondly, the theological logic is identical; both face divine chastisement while holding onto a sense of being fortunate and privileged. Thirdly, the extrapolation from individual to national is identical in both sources: the Psalm’s gever gives way to “His people” and “His inheritance,” exactly as our poem’s author attempts to extrapolate from first-person suffering to the community, who indeed responds in its plural communal voice once the gever’s speech concludes. Fourth, both counsel patience pointing to the long-term future; the Psalmist promises future quiet while the gever here too continues to bear his yoke emboldened by the certainty of YHWH’s benevolence and its ultimate emergence from hiding. Elsewhere in scripture, gever appears, even in the broader context of suffering under divine affliction as in Job (3:3, 10:5, 14:14, 33:17, 34:7), but without the many parallelisms that Psalm 94 and Eikhah 3 share. Moreover, both the Psalm and this poem end identically, with YHWH meting out punishment to evildoers.)The gever’s testimony here is deliberately extreme: he catalogues a litany of suffering that matches and perhaps exceeds the collective agonies described in the first two poems, with all rendered in the first person singular. The imagery is graphic and unsparing — bears, lions, arrows, gravel, ashes. The gever’s belief begins to waver; perhaps his hopes in the benevolence of YHWH had been ill placed. “But then I call the following to mind, and become hopeful once more.” The gever does not deny his suffering, nor does he retract his attribution of it to YHWH. Instead, he comes to reframe it. “The kindness of YHWH never ceases; His mercies are never exhausted; they return anew each morning.” This is the gever’s central and revolutionary claim: not that suffering is an illusion, not that YHWH had no hand in it, but that YHWH’s benevolence is all-pervasive and unfailing even when it appears entirely absent. This is not retrospective theodicy — not the backward-looking claim that suffering was deserved — but prospective hope: a confidence that YHWH’s goodness is unshakable, and its meaning will ultimately emerge from its present concealment. YHWH has complex long-term agendas that defy short-term mortal readings. What appears as cruelty in the present must be the necessary catalyst for grand future redemption. Ultimately, the gever counsels patience, solitary endurance, and acceptance of the yoke, because suffering has great meaning even when it is not yet visible to mortal eyes.The Adonaist’s Complementary Comfort (vv. 31–39) At this point, an Adonaist voice enters with a complementary perspective. He agrees with the gever in practice — endorsing patience and endurance — but not in theological principle. He knows nothing of grand providential schemes or mysterious long-term designs. But what he can staunchly advocate is that Adonai is fundamentally good: stern but just, and ultimately kind and merciful. God does not afflict out of desire, nor does He seek to impose grief on mortals. His punishments are educational rather than vindictive. Nothing befalls man that is undeserved. The comfort here is grounded in the conviction that Adonai’s character is good, even when His actions appear harsh. Repent and all will be well.The Community’s Failed Assimilation (vv. 40–47) A third voice, employing the plural “we,” now joins the discourse. This is the community attempting to assimilate the empowering – but conflicting – messages it has received. Both the Yahwist and Adonaist accounts now seem safer and more approachable, but they are caught between the forward-facing providence of the Yahwist and the backward-facing sin and repentance narrative of the Adonaist. Their initial words are thus promising though contradictory: “Let us survey and scrutinise our ways and return to YHWH.” But their assimilation rapidly disintegrates. What begins as an upbeat call to re-embrace YHWH degenerates into bitter resentment; their humble tone regresses into accusation. They find persecution, not restitution, in YHWH’s providence. Moreover, further Yahwist theological confusion – likely associated with earlier Yahwistic views – becomes evident as they fluctuate between conceptions of YHWH as passive and active. The failed integration testifies to the depth of their wound: the theology of comfort, however cogent in the abstract, cannot yet take root in this traumatised soil.The Final Synthesis (vv. 48–66) In response to this turmoil, the closing speaker drops the suggestion that the community bear personal responsibility for what has befallen them — a tactical retreat from the Adonaist position that likely triggered the community’s collapse. Instead, and likely in response to the Yahwist confusion too, he outlines a framework depicting YHWH as both passively withdrawn and actively providential, and demonstrates how this apparent paradox is sustaining rather than destructive. This is the poem’s most intellectually ambitious thesis: YHWH never has a hand in evil, for all evil is the consequence of withheld providence — yet YHWH has grand long-term schemes, and this horrendous episode should be reframed as vital and gestational as will one day become apparent. The two claims appear logically incompatible: if YHWH is passive, how can He have providential schemes? If He has schemes, how can He be withdrawn and uninvolved? The closing speaker does not resolve this tension; he embraces it. Perhaps certain theological paradoxes cannot be resolved rationally but must be held in tension as mysteries — a mode of thought not dissimilar to the paradoxical theology of providence later developed by Rabbi Moshe Chaim Luzzato. Simultaneously, the speaker’s anger — an inevitable emotional reaction to trauma — is no longer directed at YHWH but at the autonomous human agents of evil, those who persecuted the community of their own volition. For with YHWH absolved of perpetrating the evil, the atrocities trace back to the free will of man The poem concludes with a prayer for divine vengeance against those human oppressors.

POEM IV: Trauma31[31] The fourth poem represents a dramatic shift in register from the theological argumentation of the preceding three. Here there is no debate, no cognitive wrestling with God-concepts, no rival theological frameworks vying for supremacy. The speakers — a narrator-observer and the community — are frozen in the psychosomatic dimension of trauma: they recount scenes of starvation, degradation, and cannibalism with the numb intensity of witnesses who have not yet begun to process what they have seen. Yet the voice is undoubtedly Yahwist with YHWH cited by name, and with a strong undertone of sinfulness met by providential punishment.The Narrator’s Catalogue of Horror (vv. 1–11) The poem opens with the characteristic “How is it conceivable” (eikhah), but the question here may be more phenomenological than theological. The narrator cannot fathom the sheer facts of what has occurred. Sacred stones spattered at every street head; precious children evaluated as earthen flasks; suckling babes with tongues stuck to their palates for thirst; those reared in scarlet robes embracing trash heaps; compassionate women boiling their own children. The imagery deliberately exceeds that of the earlier poems in its visceral specificity.The Exposure of Internal Corruption (vv. 12–16) The poem’s most theologically significant contribution is its unfiltered exposure of Judea’s own moral corruption. Where the more cognitively defended speakers of earlier poems either assigned blame abstractly or directed it outward at enemies, this poem names the specific agents of a horrific internal rot: the false prophets and decadent priests who shed the blood of their righteous challengers; who staggered through the streets religiously blind while defiling themselves with innocent blood; who violently and wrongly quashed the true prophecies predicting Jerusalem’s downfall. These are details that the theologically engaged speakers of the first three poems could not articulate. No theologian had dared to suggest that indeed Judea had become more evil than the infamous Sodom. Yet, somehow, the cognitive paralysis of raw trauma permits such unflinching self-examination; for personal guilt tends to fester in the climate of traumatic shock.The Community’s Shattered Ideology (vv. 17–20) The community speaks up to emphasise the traumatisation of their worldview. Their belief in the invincibility of Jerusalem and their monarch has come crashing down. They had waited for allied saviours who never arrived; they had rested their hopes on nations who did not save them. The passage recounting the capture of “the anointed of YHWH” — the king “in whose protective shadow we said we shall live alongside the nations” — registers the collapse not merely of a political entity but of an entire theology of election. The Prophetic Coda (vv. 21–22) A brief, cold, and prophetic third voice concludes the poem with laconic assurance. Addressing Edom with biting irony — “Rejoice and be glad” — the speaker warns that the cup of wrath will pass their way too. To Zion, a single terse comfort: “Your corruption is spent; He shall exile you no more.” To Edom: “He has noted your corruption; He has exposed your sin.” The voice is impersonal, and its brevity contrasts sharply with the agonised and emotive prolixity that precedes it. It offers a theological handhold — the bare assertion that providential justice operates across nations. Its tone matches the dissociated trauma victim, who can speak the facts without emotionally registering them. Theologically, this poem displays how a prophetic theological truth can be known without being healing — that cognitive clarity and emotional devastation can coexist. The factual assertion of spent punishment sits within a register of traumatic dissociation, not of redemptive hope.
The narrator-observer begins:
How is it conceivable
That the gold has dimmed,
That the fine gold’s appearance has changed!?
That sacred stones are spattered
At every street head!?

That the precious children of Zion,
Once as grand as gold —
Are now evaluated as earthen flasks,
The work of a potter’s hands!

That even the jackals proffer the breast
As they nurse their young pups,
Yet my community has become selfishly callous;
Abandoning their young
like the ostriches in the wilderness.

That the tongue of the suckling babe
Sticks to its palate for thirst;
That the young children beg for bread,
But no one provides them.

That those who feasted on delicacies
Now perish in the streets;
That those reared in scarlet robes
Now embrace the trash heap.

That the sin of my community
Has exceeded the sin of Sodom;
For it only suffered momentarily:
Overturned in an instant,
With no human hand laid on it.

That her princes —
Their white hues once purer than snow,
Whiter than milk,
Their red hues once ruddier than rubies,
Their forms once like artisan-cut sapphire —

But now their appearance is blacker than soot;
They are unrecognisable in the streets.
Their skin has shrivelled on their bodies;
Having become as dry as wood.

That the victims of the sword were better off
Than the victims of hunger,
For once stabbed — their blood drained with haste,
And at least they were sated with the produce of the field.

Conversely, among the victims of hunger:
The hands of compassionate women
Boiled their own children.
They became foodstuff for their mothers
As my community broke down.

That YHWH exploded all His wrath;
Pouring out His burning anger.
That He kindled a fire in Zion
Consuming its very foundations.

The kings of the land,
Along with all civilization’s inhabitants,
Once thought it impossible
For oppressor or enemy
to enter the gates of Jerusalem.

But now, due to her false prophets’ sins,
And her decadent priests’ corruption,
Who shed the blood of their righteous challengers
In her midst —

The religiously blind staggered through the streets,
Defiling themselves with so much righteous blood,
That no one could touch their blood-soaked garments.

"Away! Unclean Ones!", they cried out to the righteous;
"Away! Away! Do not touch the sanctum!"
They would cry as they fluttered and staggered about;
Stating adamantly that the Judeans shall never again live exiled among the nations.

O, how zealously they quashed the true prophecies predicting Jerusalem’s downfall!
YHWH has providentially scattered them;
He shall no longer behold their plight;
For they had no regard for the righteous priests,
Nor grace for the scholarly elders.

The community speaks, their shattered ideology laid bare — their belief in Jerusalem’s invincibility has collapsed: 32[32] Markers of voice shift: the grammatical person switches to first-person plural (“our eyes,” “we remained,” “our helpers”).
As long as we remained in Jerusalem,
We bought into their false utopian vision:
Our eyes looked out for our helpers —
Ultimately in vain;
We rested our hopes on an allied nation —
Ultimately it would not save us.

Thus our enemies closed in,
They stalked our movements,
They scared us from walking our streets.
We sensed that our end was nigh;
That our days were numbered,
And then — that our end had arrived.

Suddenly,
Our pursuers swooped upon us,
Swifter than the eagles in the heavens;
They chased us on the mountains;
They lay in wait for us in the wilderness.

Even our breath of life —
The current of our nostrils,
The anointed of YHWH
Fell into their snares —
He of whom we said:
"In his protective shadow
We shall live alongside the nations".

A cold, prophetic voice concludes the poem:33[33] Markers of voice shift: the addressee changes abruptly from the audience to speaking imperatively a third party – Edom, before the speaker turns to address to the community in the second person, confirming that this voice belongs to someone other than the community.
Rejoice and be glad
Community of Edom
Residents of the land of Uz.
For the cup of wrath (Jer. 25:25–27) shall pass your way too;
You shall be drunk,
You shall be sickened,
You shall retch.

Community of Zion:
Your corruption is spent,
He shall exile you no more.
Community of Edom:
He has noted your corruption,
He has exposed your sin.

Lamentations 5:1 POEM V: The Prayer34[34] The fifth and final poem is more prayer than poem. Alone among the five, it is addressed entirely and directly to YHWH — a unified communal voice speaking in the second person throughout. The theological anxieties explored discretely in the preceding poems are here calmed in a single sustained address, until the poem’s devastating final section retroactively destabilises all prior attempt at resolution.The Catalogue of Degradation (vv. 1–18) The community describes its present condition to YHWH in graphic but measured detail. The tone is neither accusatory nor supplicatory but reportorial — a calm, exhaustive inventory of loss. Ancestral lands turned over to strangers; homes given to aliens; the community reduced to orphans without a father, widows without a husband. Water that was once their own must now be purchased; wood comes at a price. They are yoked and hounded, weary and offered no rest. The passage sweeps through economic deprivation, political subjugation, physical violence, sexual assault, and the humiliation of the elderly and the young, building a comprehensive portrait of total devastation. This extensive report is framed within their passive Yahwist theology, that YHWH withdrew and failed to take notice of all that befell the community. The Theological Pivot and Devastating Close (vv. 19–22) In its closing lines, the prayer turns to overt theology, asserting that YHWH is an eternal presence whose throne — omnipotence over the earthly realm — endures from generation to generation. But if so, continues the poet: “Why have You forgotten us for what seems like eternity? Why have You forsaken us for so many days?” These closing questions are the sharpest and most direct of the entire work, unequivocally framing the work as a struggle with theodicy: just as Eikhah opens with the bewildered cry “Eikhah” — “How is it conceivable?” — so it closes with an equally urgent theological question. This framing constitutes perhaps the strongest evidence that Eikhah is fundamentally a vehicle for posing the question of national theodicy.The prayer’s penultimate verse is a straightforward petition for restoration, communicating the community’s remaining vestiges of Yahwist hope: “Restore us to yourself, YHWH, that we may be restored; renew our days as of old.” But then, the ultimate verse delivers a twist that shatters this hope and reverberates backward through the entire work. For just a moment, we glimpse an additional, suppressed and hitherto theologically inconceivable hypothesis, that perhaps their ongoing suffering points to a God has come to hates His people, to abandon them forever! But this hypothesis too is rapidly rejected, “For even if You deeply despised us, You unleashed your fury against us to the extreme.” In other words, once more, paradoxical Yahwism comes to the fore: the ongoing and extreme experiences of the Judeans indicate that they were not merely victim to natural processes in the absence of YHWH’s protection, but rather, that YHWH was providentially albeit painfully steering their destiny throughout. Thus, their suffering is as much testament to their unbreakable covenant with YHWH as their former success. Nonetheless, the sudden appearance of these verses just as the work winds to its close signals that unsettled doubts about God’s disposition towards Israel continue to haunt the community. That the grappling with national theodicy prayer ends not with resolution but with an open wound. For perhaps it is impossible to satisfactorily settle the question of whether YHWH withdrew or attacked.
Be mindful, O YHWH, of what has befallen us;
Behold and see our disgrace!

Lamentations 5:22 For even if35[35] The Hebrew “ki im” is rendered here as “for even if.” The verse’s main thrust is that the biting question of “why” cannot be resolved by claiming that God acted out of hateful rejection, for the ongoing and extreme nature of the suffering points to deliberate, providential and unfinished business. The question therefore returns, unanswerable. Note however, that the very entertaining the possibility that God might despise His people signals unsettled doubts about God’s disposition towards Israel. Other commentators have used an alternative rendering, “unless You have utterly rejected us”. This maintains the doubt while ending with the community’s floated answer rather than leaving the question open whichever way one looks at it. You deeply despised us,
You unleashed your fury against us to the extreme.
